summary: Iteration 4 tested NSGA-II vs random search on a reduced parameter space (900 configs) and compared against the full space. The main convergence advantage of NSGA-II was confirmed (47-eval gap to 95% HV), but the critical surprise was that the reduced space itself was flawed: block_size=32 (excluded as 'non-differentiating') actually doubles effective KV token capacity at high TP, causing full-space NSGA-II to exceed the reduced-space exhaustive Pareto front by 10.4%.
key_points: Robustness arm: Pareto density was 26.4% (238/900 non-dominated), slightly above the predicted 8-25% range, spanning all 4 GPU tiers with genuine within-tier tradeoffs confirmed.

Main arm (partially confirmed): NSGA-II reached 95% of exhaustive HV at eval=117 vs random at eval=164 (47-eval gap). At eval=80: NSGA-II=91.2% (predicted ≥93%), random=88.6% (predicted ≤88%). Final NSGA-II HV=97.8% of exhaustive at 200 evals.

Ablation arm (REFUTED): Full-space NSGA-II achieved HV=5.85e10, exceeding the reduced-space exhaustive front (5.30e10) by 10.4%. Root cause: block_size_in_tokens=32 eliminates preemptions at tp=8 (107→0 preemptions, ttft_p99 2323ms→25ms) because total KV capacity = blocks × block_size (96k vs 48k tokens at kv=3000).
Key lesson: block_size_in_tokens is a critical parameter for high-TP configurations and must remain in the search space. The earlier probing at tp=2 missed this regime-dependent interaction.
Control arm (confirmed): Random search reached 95% at eval=164 (predicted ≥160), final HV=96.1% of exhaustive, validating it as appropriate baseline.
